body:
The emergence of the Sikh tradition

The Sikh tradition developed in Punjab during a period when Bhakti saints and Sufi teachers were questioning rigid social distinctions and emphasising devotion to God. Its foundation is associated with Guru Nanak (1469–1539), the first of the 10 Sikh Gurus.

Guru Nanak was born at Talwandi, now known as Nankana Sahib in Pakistan. He travelled widely to communicate his teachings and later established a community at Kartarpur, near the river Ravi. His teachings, the institutions developed by his successors and the preservation of their sacred compositions gradually gave the Sikh community a distinct identity.

Guru: A spiritual teacher or guide. In Sikh history, the expression 10 Sikh Gurus refers to the recognised line of human Gurus from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh. The Guru Granth Sahib subsequently received the status of eternal Guru.

Guru Nanak's central teachings

Guru Nanak taught devotion to one supreme, formless God. His teachings are associated with nirguna bhakti, or devotion to the Divine without a physical form or attributes of an embodied deity. He opposed the idea that outward rituals, caste status or priestly mediation were necessary for spiritual liberation.

He emphasised that devotion should shape everyday conduct. A person could lead a household life, work honestly, remember God and serve others. Spiritual life was therefore not restricted to renunciation or withdrawal from society.

Three principles commonly used to summarise his teachings

  • Naam Japna: Remembering and meditating upon the Divine Name. It expresses continuous awareness of God rather than dependence on outward ritual alone.
  • Kirat Karna: Earning a livelihood through honest work. Productive work and moral conduct are compatible with spiritual life.
  • Vand Chhakna: Sharing one's earnings and resources with others, especially those in need. It connects personal devotion with social responsibility.

Sangat, kirtan and langar

Guru Nanak organised his followers into a community. Its practices helped turn shared religious ideas into a continuing social tradition.

  • Sangat: A congregation of devotees who assemble for collective worship, reflection and the singing or recitation of sacred hymns.
  • Shabad and kirtan: A shabad is a sacred hymn or composition. Kirtan is the devotional singing of such hymns. Guru Nanak sang his compositions in musical modes known as ragas; his companion Bhai Mardana accompanied him on the rabab, a stringed instrument.
  • Langar: A community kitchen and shared meal. People could sit and eat together regardless of caste, former religious affiliation or gender. The practice expressed equality through participation in ordinary social life.
  • Dharamsal: The early place of Sikh religious assembly associated with Guru Nanak's community. The Sikh place of worship later came to be known as a gurdwara.

These institutions are related but not interchangeable. Sangat refers to the congregation, langar to the shared kitchen and meal, and gurdwara to the place of Sikh worship.

Succession to Guru Angad

Before his death in 1539, Guru Nanak selected his disciple Lehna as successor. Lehna became known as Guru Angad, the second Sikh Guru. This established the continuation of spiritual leadership through successive Gurus.

The Sikh tradition did not depend only on the life of its founder. Subsequent Gurus preserved the teachings, developed community institutions and contributed compositions that would eventually form the Guru Granth Sahib.

Prelims focus

  • Guru Nanak: 1st Sikh Guru; lived from 1469 to 1539.
  • Birthplace: Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan.
  • Important early community centre: Kartarpur, near the Ravi.
  • Guru Nanak's companion Bhai Mardana played the rabab.
  • Lehna became the 2nd Guru, Guru Angad.
  • Trap: Sangat means congregation; langar means the community kitchen and shared meal.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, chapter Devotional Paths to the Divine, printed pp. 117–119; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, chapter Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, section 8.2, printed p. 163; Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC), Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji and Ten Guru Sahibs, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Langar brought people together through a shared meal, regardless of social background.

title: Guru Nanak and the Foundations of the Sikh Tradition

body:
Continuity after Guru Nanak

After Guru Nanak's death in 1539, the next 4 Gurus continued his teachings and strengthened the organisation of the Sikh community. Their contributions included the development of a writing tradition, centres of worship, community kitchens and, eventually, a collected scripture.

The central distinction is that Guru Angad developed the use of Gurmukhi for preserving teachings, Guru Amar Das strengthened community institutions, Guru Ram Das developed the settlement that became Amritsar, and Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth in 1604.

The 2nd to 5th Sikh Gurus

GuruKey contributionImportant association
2. Guru AngadStandardised and popularised the Gurmukhi script; collected Guru Nanak's hymns; expanded langar and education.Khadur Sahib; Gurmukhi
3. Guru Amar DasStrengthened langar and organised preaching through 22 centres called manjis; encouraged social equality and reform.Goindwal; pangat and sangat
4. Guru Ram DasDeveloped Ramdaspur, which became Amritsar; promoted work on the sacred pool; composed the 4 Laavan hymns.Ramdaspur or Amritsar
5. Guru ArjanCompiled the Adi Granth in 1604; developed Harmandir Sahib as a major Sikh centre.Amritsar; Adi Granth

Guru Angad and the Gurmukhi script

Guru Angad continued the teachings of Guru Nanak and contributed his own compositions. He is especially associated with the development and popularisation of Gurmukhi, using and modifying an earlier regional writing tradition to provide a recognisable script for Sikh religious literature.

A script and a language are different concepts. Gurmukhi is a writing system, not a language. It is used to write Punjabi and to preserve the Sikh sacred compositions. This distinction becomes important when studying the Guru Granth Sahib, which contains material with diverse linguistic influences.

Guru Amar Das: equality through community practice

Guru Amar Das established his principal centre at Goindwal. He strengthened the institution of langar and emphasised that visitors should join the common meal before meeting the Guru. This practice is expressed through the traditional phrase Pehle Pangat, Phir Sangat, meaning that the shared meal comes before joining the religious assembly.

Pangat refers to the line or gathering in which people sit together to eat. Sangat refers to the congregation. Eating together helped challenge the social separation created by caste distinctions.

Guru Amar Das also organised 22 manjis, or preaching centres, to extend the activities of the Sikh community. He opposed social practices such as sati and purdah and supported greater dignity for women.

Guru Ram Das and the development of Amritsar

Guru Ram Das established the settlement known as Chak Ramdas or Ramdaspur, which developed into Amritsar. Work on the sacred pool helped the settlement become a major Sikh religious centre.

He also composed the 4 Laavan hymns, associated with the Sikh marriage ceremony. These are part of his contribution to Sikh religious literature.

Amritsar association: Guru Ram Das is associated with founding and developing the settlement. Guru Arjan is associated with the development of Harmandir Sahib and the installation of the Adi Granth there in 1604.

Guru Arjan and the Adi Granth

Guru Arjan, the fifth Sikh Guru, brought together compositions of the preceding Gurus, his own hymns and the works of selected devotional poets. The resulting compilation, completed in 1604, is known as the Adi Granth.

Bhai Gurdas served as the scribe of the compilation. The Adi Granth was installed at Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, and Baba Buddha became its first granthi, or custodian and reader of the scripture.

The original compilation and its later development into the Guru Granth Sahib are connected stages in the history of the same sacred textual tradition. The details of the scripture's later additions are explained separately.

The death of Guru Arjan in 1606

Guru Arjan was executed in 1606 during the reign of the Mughal emperor Jahangir. This event marked an important change in the historical circumstances of the Sikh community. Under the next Guru, Hargobind, spiritual leadership became more explicitly associated with the community's responsibility for its public security and collective affairs.

Prelims focus

  • Guru Angad: 2nd Guru; associated with Gurmukhi.
  • Guru Amar Das: 3rd Guru; Goindwal, langar and 22 manjis.
  • Guru Ram Das: 4th Guru; Ramdaspur or Amritsar and the 4 Laavan.
  • Guru Arjan: 5th Guru; compiled the Adi Granth in 1604.
  • Bhai Gurdas: scribe; Baba Buddha: first granthi.
  • Trap: The original compilation of 1604 was made by Guru Arjan, not Guru Gobind Singh.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, chapter Devotional Paths to the Divine, printed pp. 117–118; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, section 8.2, printed pp. 163–164; SGPC, Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji, Sri Guru Amar Das Ji, Sri Guru Ram Das Ji, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji and Sri Guru Granth Sahib, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Anonymous Punjabi scribes copy manuscripts with reed pens in an Amritsar courtyard, with stacked folios and cloth-wrapped bundles nearby.
pictures.caption: The collection and copying of hymns made an organised Sikh scripture possible.

title: Gurus Angad to Arjan: Institutions, Settlements and the First Compilation

body:
Changes after 1606

The execution of Guru Arjan in 1606 occurred at a time of increasing tension between the Sikh community and Mughal authority. The next Gurus continued the spiritual tradition while responding to changing social and political circumstances. Their contributions should be understood as developments within the same line of Sikh Guruship, not as the beginning of a separate religious tradition.

The 6th to 9th Sikh Gurus

GuruPrincipal associationKey fact
6. Guru HargobindMiri-Piri; Akal TakhtEmphasised spiritual and temporal responsibility; established the Akal Takht at Amritsar in 1609.
7. Guru Har RaiKiratpur; service and compassionMaintained the Sikh community's organisation and is remembered for herbal medicine and care for the sick.
8. Guru Har KrishanChild Guru; DelhiBecame Guru at about 5 years of age; remembered for helping sufferers during an epidemic in Delhi.
9. Guru Tegh BahadurChak Nanki; martyrdomFounded the settlement later known as Anandpur Sahib; executed in Delhi in 1675; his hymns entered the later Guru Granth Sahib.

Guru Hargobind: Miri and Piri

Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru, is associated with the concept of Miri-Piri. This teaching expresses the relationship between spiritual guidance and responsibility for the affairs and protection of the community.

  • Piri: Spiritual authority, religious life and guidance.
  • Miri: Temporal or worldly authority, including public responsibility and the protection of the community.

Guru Hargobind symbolised these 2 responsibilities through the wearing of 2 swords. The idea did not replace the spiritual teachings of Guru Nanak; it connected those teachings with the need to address the community's circumstances.

The Akal Takht

Guru Hargobind established the Akal Takht at Amritsar in 1609. It developed as an important centre for the community's collective affairs and authority. It stands in close association with Harmandir Sahib, which had become the central place for the Sikh scripture and worship.

Distinguish the institutions: Harmandir Sahib is the major Sikh shrine associated with worship and the installation of the Adi Granth. Akal Takht, established by Guru Hargobind, is associated particularly with the collective authority and public affairs of the Sikh Panth.

Guru Har Rai: continuity and service

Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, continued the religious and organisational institutions of his predecessors. Although he retained the community's capacity for defence, he is principally remembered for his peaceful disposition, compassion and service.

He is associated with Kiratpur and with the use of medicinal plants and a dispensary for treating the sick. His contribution illustrates that the Sikh tradition combined spiritual instruction with practical assistance to people.

Guru Har Krishan: the child Guru

Guru Har Krishan, the eighth Guru, succeeded Guru Har Rai in 1661 when he was about 5 years old. He is therefore remembered as the child Guru.

During his stay in Delhi, an epidemic affected the population. Sikh tradition remembers him for assisting sufferers without discrimination. He died in 1664 while still a child.

Guru Tegh Bahadur: religious freedom and scripture

Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, established Chak Nanki, the settlement later known as Anandpur Sahib. He travelled to strengthen Sikh religious communities and composed devotional hymns.

He was executed in Delhi in 1675 during the reign of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. Sikh tradition especially remembers his martyrdom in connection with the defence of freedom of religious belief, including the protection sought by Kashmiri Hindus.

His compositions are important for the history of the sacred scripture. They were not part of Guru Arjan's original compilation of 1604; they were incorporated into the later form of the Guru Granth Sahib under Guru Gobind Singh.

Prelims focus

  • Guru Hargobind: 6th Guru; Miri-Piri and Akal Takht, 1609.
  • Guru Har Rai: 7th Guru; associated with Kiratpur, compassion and care for the sick.
  • Guru Har Krishan: 8th Guru; became Guru at about 5 years of age and died in 1664.
  • Guru Tegh Bahadur: 9th Guru; associated with Chak Nanki, martyrdom in 1675 and hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib.
  • Trap: The Akal Takht was established by Guru Hargobind, not Guru Arjan.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, chapter Devotional Paths to the Divine, printed p. 118; SGPC, Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, Sri Guru Har Rai Ji, Sri Guru Har Krishan Ji, Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji and Sri Akal Takht Sahib, consulted 20 November 2026; Sikh Missionary Society, In the Guru's Footsteps, chapter Guru Har Rai, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Guru Hargobind's 2 swords represent Piri, spiritual guidance, and Miri, public responsibility, linked within Sikh leadership.
pictures.caption: Miri and Piri express the linked temporal and spiritual responsibilities associated with Guru Hargobind.

title: Gurus Hargobind to Tegh Bahadur: Spiritual Leadership and Public Responsibility
